title: Air conditioning was for paper
hook: The first modern air conditioner was built to keep paper flat, not people cool.
peek: In 1902 a young engineer named Willis Carrier designed a machine for a Brooklyn printing plant. Its job was to control humidity, so the paper would stop swelling and the coloured inks would line up. Cooling people came later.
lede: In 1902 the Sackett-Wilhelms printing company in Brooklyn had a problem. Humid summer air made its paper swell and shrink, so each colour, printed in a separate pass, landed slightly out of line. Willis Carrier, a 25-year-old engineer at the Buffalo Forge Company, designed a system that blew air over chilled coils to pull moisture out of it.

bullets.text: Carrier's insight was that chilling air to a set temperature fixes how much water it can hold. By cooling air to a chosen dew point, he could set the humidity in the room. The cooling itself was almost a side effect.
Carrier later said the idea came together one foggy night on a railway platform in Pittsburgh, while he thought about how fog forms when air holds all the water it can.
Carrier did not invent the phrase. Stuart Cramer, an engineer who controlled humidity in textile mills, used the term air conditioning in 1906, and Carrier later adopted it.
Comfort cooling arrived in the 1920s. In 1925 a Carrier system was switched on at the Rivoli Theatre in New York, and cinemas soon advertised being cool inside to draw summer crowds.
